headline: Agent suites deliver ROI and quietly threaten per-seat SaaS, shifting to usage-based pricing
summary: Companies adopting packaged agent suites are seeing significant ROI, but this also converts traditional seat-based SaaS spend into usage/outcome fees, leading to a reduction in human seats.
details: Buying packaged agent suites offers a dual advantage: faster production and measurable ROI. However, this also quietly threatens traditional per-seat SaaS models by converting spend into usage or outcome-based fees, ultimately reducing human seat requirements.

While companies often frame 'build vs. buy' as an engineering trade-off, the business reality is sharper. MIT Project NANDA reported 95% of GenAI pilots yield no material return, contrasting with BCG's 5% club capturing most gains, pushing leaders to consider vendor agents over internal platforms.

Real-world examples demonstrate this shift: Salesforce's Agentforce reached $800M ARR and saw a ~10% seat reduction per service agent within 12 months. ServiceNow's Now Assist also more than doubled net-new ACV YoY in Q4 FY25, crediting agentic AI for production deployments.

River Group/Deloitte documented agentic deployments in banking achieving 200–2,000% productivity gains for KYC/AML tasks. Internal builds often fail at the pilot-to-production stage due to a lack of robust production systems like evaluation harnesses, observability, and governance, which vendors include.

CFOs can estimate seat-risk using a simple three-line model: identify candidate seat pools (repeatable tasks), apply an adoption ramp (e.g., 20-40% in year 1), and convert displaced seats to outcome ARR by modeling a replacement rate for usage fees.

For a 1,000-seat support org paying $6k/seat/year, if 30% of seats are automatable and agents capture 30% adoption in year 1, 90 seats are displaced. This represents $540k of seat ARR at risk, with an estimated $216k recaptured as outcome ARR, leading to a net loss of $324k in seat ARR.

Not all seats are at risk; complex or emotionally charged interactions still require human oversight, as Klarna's experience showed. However, buying packaged agents is often the fastest path to production and measurable ROI, driving a significant shift from per-seat licensing to usage/outcome pricing that financial models must now explicitly address.

headline_marked: [[A single JPEG file can hide up to 90 frames]] for a full video, exploiting progressive scan features
headline: A single JPEG file can hide up to 90 frames for a full video, exploiting progressive scan features
summary: Researchers discovered how to manipulate JPEG progressive scans to embed sequential images, effectively creating a multi-frame animation or video within one file.
details: Progressive JPEG files display a low-resolution version first, then refine the image as more data downloads. This works by breaking compressed data into multiple "scans," each adding more detail.
An initial attempt involved concatenating multiple single-scan JPEGs. However, most decoders stop processing after a certain number of scans, typically limiting this method to around 9 frames.
A refined technique uses "DC-only" scans, which are standards-compliant and contain only the lowest frequency data. This avoids issues with AC scans refining old data, preventing "ghosting" effects.

This method allows packing up to 90 frames into a single JPEG file, with Chrome rendering around this many and Firefox showing even more. The process involves using `jpegtran` with custom scan definitions.
While lacking practical applications due to no timing information, it enables creative uses like unconventional rickrolls, partial rendering effects, or even interactive single-page applications.
caption:
Did you know a single JPEG image can hide an entire video? A clever manipulation of progressive JPEG scans allows embedding up to 90 sequential frames.

Progressive JPEG files display a low-resolution version first, then refine the image as more data downloads. This works by breaking compressed data into multiple "scans," each adding more detail.

An initial attempt involved concatenating multiple single-scan JPEGs. However, most decoders stop processing after a certain number of scans, typically limiting this method to around 9 frames.

A refined technique uses "DC-only" scans, which are standards-compliant and contain only the lowest frequency data. This avoids issues with AC scans refining old data, preventing "ghosting" effects.

This method allows packing up to 90 frames into a single JPEG file, with Chrome rendering around this many and Firefox showing even more. The process involves using `jpegtran` with custom scan definitions.

While lacking practical applications due to no timing information, it enables creative uses like unconventional rickrolls, partial rendering effects, or even interactive single-page applications.
